title: Fix 'Too many levels of symbolic links' by finding and removing a symlink loop
summary: A symbolic link (a shortcut) points to another link that leads back to itself, so the system never reaches a real file and gives up. Find the looping link, check where it points, then remove it or point it at the real file.
error_patterns: Too many levels of symbolic links

aliases.text: too many levels of symbolic links
cat too many levels of symbolic links
ошибка too many levels of symbolic links

prerequisites: Know the folder where the error appears, or use your home folder
Know the file or program that printed the error

steps.explain: List the broken symbolic links in a folder. A loop shows up here too, because it never reaches a real file. Nothing is changed by this command.

placeholders.name: DIR
placeholders.description: Folder to search, for example your home folder or the folder with the error

steps.expect: One or more paths, one per line, e.g. /home/user/projects/link1. Loops and plain broken links both appear. Nothing printed: try another DIR.

alternatives.explain: Search the whole disk for broken links. This is slower and may print many permission errors, which can be ignored.

steps.explain: Show where the link points. ls -l does not follow the link, so it works even for a loop. Read the text after the arrow ->: if it points to another link in the list, and that link points back, you have found the loop.

placeholders.name: LINK
placeholders.description: Path of the looping link found in the previous step

steps.expect: A line that starts with l, for example lrwxrwxrwx 1 user user 8 Oct 24 13:25 /home/user/projects/link1 -> /home/user/projects/link2. Note the path after -> : you will need it as TARGET.

alternatives.explain: Print only the path the link points to, without the other columns.
alternatives.expect: One path, for example /home/user/projects/link2. If the output is another link, which points back, it is a loop.

steps.explain: Remove the looping link. This deletes only the shortcut, never the file it points to. Write down the path from step 2 first, so you can restore the link if needed.

placeholders.name: LINK
placeholders.description: Path of the looping link to remove

steps.expect: No output. The command returns to the prompt. The link is gone.

alternatives.explain: Keep the link but point it at the real file instead of the loop. Use this when a program expects the link to exist.

placeholders.name: REAL_FILE
placeholders.description: The real file or folder the link should point to

placeholders.name: LINK
placeholders.description: Path of the looping link to replace

alternatives.expect: No output. Check with ls -l <LINK>: the arrow now points to REAL_FILE.

verify.expect: The looping link is gone. If another link from the same pair is still listed, it is now broken: remove it the same way.

rollback.explain: Restore the link with the target you wrote down in step 2. Use this if you removed or re-pointed a link by mistake.

placeholders.name: TARGET
placeholders.description: The path the link pointed to before the change (the text after -> in step 2)

placeholders.name: LINK
placeholders.description: Path of the link to restore

rollback.expect: No output. ls -l <LINK> shows the old target again.

warnings: Remove only the link, never the folder it lives in. Use rm without -r; rm -r on a link to a folder can delete the folder's contents.
Do not remove a link inside a system folder such as /usr, /etc or /lib unless a program you installed created it. Those links belong to installed packages.
If the link keeps coming back, a program is recreating it. Find that program before you remove the link again.
Removing one link of a loop can leave the other link broken. Run the find command again and remove the leftover link too, if no program needs it.

source.title: find manual; card written and verified in the lnxhelp sandbox
